title: Understanding HTTP Status Code Classes
learning_outcomes: Explain how understanding http status code classes affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from informational responses to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on understanding http status code classes in http status codes and response headers. You will connect informational responses to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding HTTP Status Code Classes matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying informational responses deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Status codes carry protocol-level meaning; headers and structured bodies add metadata needed by clients. In this lesson, treat “Understanding HTTP Status Code Classes” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.test/problems/state-conflict",
  "title": "State conflict",

  "detail": "The order cannot be cancelled after dispatch."
}
content_blocks.expected_output: The status gives generic protocol meaning; problem details explain the application-specific conflict without exposing internal traces.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Informational responses”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Successful responses” and “Server errors”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Choose a status from the operation outcome, not from how easy it is to implement. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating understanding http status code classes as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
